advance-directives-and-surrogates.name: Advance directives and surrogate decisions
advance-directives-and-surrogates.scope: Living will, DNR/DNI orders, health care proxy, substituted judgment, best interests, advance care planning
advance-directives-and-surrogates.core: Follow the capable patient's current wishes; when capacity is absent, use valid directives and authorized surrogate judgment.

rows.label: Principle
items: Autonomy persists after incapacity through documented preferences and legally authorized decision-makers
Substituted judgment: patient's known values; best interests: benefits/burdens when preferences unknown

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Confirm capacity, directive validity, clinical applicability, and designated **health care proxy**
★ Apply the patient's instructions over conflicting surrogate preferences
Discuss goals, code status, surrogate early; terminal sole caregiver → plan **child guardianship**

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ **DNR limits CPR**; do not automatically withhold antibiotics, analgesia, nutrition, or other treatment
Dementia diagnosis, mild test errors, or disagreement ≠ incapacity; capacity is decision-specific
★ **Surrogate cannot compel contraindicated treatment** → withhold it; ethics consult unnecessary

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Capable patient may revise prior instructions; current informed choices control
No directive/proxy → adult next of kin; none eligible (minor relative) → **court guardian**
Clear directive/reported wishes/proxy–team agreement → no consult; unresolved conflict → ethics, court

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **DNI and DNR differ**; clarify acceptable ventilation and perioperative plans
Proxy needs no terminal illness; dementia tube-feeding request → review lack of benefit, harms
Surrogate conveys patient's known wishes, not own beliefs; missing paperwork doesn't block them

antipsychotics.name: Antipsychotics
antipsychotics.scope: First-generation vs second-generation, extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, QTc prolongation
antipsychotics.core: Dopamine-modulating drugs treat psychosis and mania; selection depends on motor, metabolic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and hematologic risks.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Psychosis, mania, agitation; **SGA first-line**; **clozapine** if resistant or recurrent suicidality
FGA: mainly D2 antagonism; SGA: D2/5-HT2 effects, varying by agent
Quetiapine sedation → switch to aripiprazole; obesity → ziprasidone, not olanzapine/clozapine

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Nigrostriatal blockade → movement disorders; tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin elevation
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist; haloperidol high-potency FGA, chlorpromazine low-potency FGA
Chronic D2 blockade → receptor supersensitivity → tardive dyskinesia; can worsen after stopping

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Fever, **lead-pipe rigidity**, autonomic instability, high CK → NMS; stop drug, supportive ICU care
Severe NMS: dantrolene/bromocriptine; olanzapine/clozapine: weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia
Risperidone: ↑prolactin; ziprasidone: ↑QT; clozapine: neutropenia, myocarditis, ileus, seizures

rows.label: Avoid
items: Lewy body/Parkinson disease: severe sensitivity; specialist-selected quetiapine/clozapine if essential
Dementia: ↑mortality, falls; dangerous behavior after safer measures → low-dose **quetiapine**/risperidone, not benzodiazepines

rows.label: Interactions
items: Other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte depletion → torsades; sedatives/alcohol increase CNS depression
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine block dopamine: same EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS; avoid after NMS

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Weight/BMI, BP, glucose/A1c, lipids; movement examinations; **ANC with clozapine**
ECG for cardiac/QT risks; prolactin when symptomatic; ask about bowel function
Clozapine + ANC <1000 → **hold clozapine**, not dose reduction; ANC 1000–1499 → continue, closer monitoring

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia**; valbenazine/deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors
Akathisia can mimic worsening agitation; increasing antipsychotic dose can worsen it
Low-potency FGAs: more orthostasis/anticholinergic effects; high-potency FGAs: more EPS

brain-abscess.name: Brain abscess
brain-abscess.scope: Direct spread (otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis), hematogenous spread (endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease), ring-enhancing lesion, polymicrobial, aspiration, empiric antibiotics
brain-abscess.core: Headache with a focal deficit or seizure and an enhancing intracranial mass after infection should prompt urgent abscess evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe or cerebellum; sinusitis/dental infection → frontal lobe
Endocarditis, cyanotic congenital heart disease, pulmonary infection → hematogenous seeding, often multiple lesions
Neurosurgery/penetrating trauma → staphylococci; immunosuppression → fungi, Nocardia, Toxoplasma

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever may be absent; nausea, papilledema or deteriorating consciousness suggest increased ICP
★ **Ring enhancement with central diffusion restriction** strongly favors pyogenic abscess

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal cerebritis progresses to encapsulated pus with surrounding vasogenic edema
Contiguous infections often polymicrobial: streptococci and anaerobes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI with DWI** preferred; contrast CT if MRI unavailable
Blood cultures before antibiotics; aspirated material → aerobic/anaerobic cultures and targeted molecular testing
★ **Avoid LP**: low diagnostic yield, mass-effect herniation risk
Search source: ENT/dental assessment; echocardiography for bacteremia, multiple lesions, or endocarditis signs

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Ceftriaxone + metronidazole**; add vancomycin for trauma, neurosurgery, or staphylococcal concern
Urgent neurosurgical aspiration/drainage for sizable accessible lesions, mass effect, or diagnostic uncertainty
Small stable lesions may receive antibiotics with serial MRI; usual IV course 6–8 weeks
Stable, aspiration within 24 hours → cultures first may be reasonable; never delay antibiotics if deteriorating
Dexamethasone only for severe edema/impending herniation; levetiracetam for seizures

rows.label: Complications
items: Intraventricular rupture, ventriculitis, herniation, persistent focal deficits, epilepsy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat contiguous infection and endocarditis; correct infectious source and relevant cardiac lesions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Necrotic tumor: central diffusion restriction less typical, no infectious source
Toxoplasmosis: advanced HIV, multiple basal ganglia lesions
Neurocysticercosis: cyst with scolex, exposure in endemic region

brain-death.name: Brain death
brain-death.scope: Prerequisites (normothermia, normal BP), clinical exam (coma, absent brainstem reflexes), apnea test, ancillary testing (cerebral blood flow studies)
brain-death.core: Permanent loss of all brain function, including brainstem function, constitutes death; a beating heart on ventilation does not negate the diagnosis.

rows.label: Principle
items: Known catastrophic irreversible brain injury; compatible neuroimaging; adequate observation period
No family consent needed; after declaration → stop ventilator, unless organ donation planned

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Prerequisites: **temperature ≥36°C**, adult SBP ≥100 and MAP ≥75 mm Hg
Exclude paralysis/metabolic confounders; sedatives: ≥5 half-lives, longer if impaired clearance
★ Examination: **coma**, no brain-mediated motor response; absent brainstem reflexes (table)

rows.label: Don't
items: Oculocephalic testing with possible cervical injury; use caloric testing after confirming ear integrity
Declare death with any brain-mediated response or spontaneous breath
Use ancillary testing to bypass hypothermia or high CNS-depressant levels

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Spinal reflex movements may persist without contradicting diagnosis
Incomplete examination or unsafe apnea test → radionuclide cerebral perfusion or catheter angiography
After temperature ≤35.5°C, wait ≥24 hours following rewarming to ≥36°C

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Apnea test: no breaths, **PaCO2 ≥60 and ≥20 above baseline**, pH <7.30
Preoxygenate; abort apnea testing for hypotension, hypoxemia or unstable arrhythmia
★ 2023 update: **EEG no longer accepted** as ancillary testing; pediatric requirements differ

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal → personality change; posterior fossa → ataxia; temporal (Meyer loop) → contralateral **superior quadrantanopia**
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus
★ **Anosmia**, normal nasal exam, frontal release signs, papilledema → **subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion
Astrocytoma grade, prognosis → **degree of histologic anaplasia**, not metastasis; extracranial spread rare

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Tinnitus, imbalance, facial weakness/numbness, altered taste (CN VII, V) → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children
Craniopharyngioma resection disrupts pituitary stalk → **lifelong pituitary hormone replacement**; watch central DI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution; chronic subdural: prior head trauma
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss

carbon-monoxide-poisoning.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.scope: Carboxyhemoglobin, pulse oximetry pitfall, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen indications, delayed neurologic sequelae
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.core: Headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion affecting several people in an enclosed combustion setting suggests carbon monoxide exposure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: House fires, faulty heaters, generators indoors, vehicle exhaust, poorly ventilated fuel-burning equipment
Pregnancy, infancy, anemia, and cardiopulmonary disease increase vulnerability at a given exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Odorless gas: flulike illness without fever; symptoms improve outside exposure site
★ **Syncope, altered consciousness, focal deficits, chest pain**, or severe acidosis → serious toxicity
**Cherry-red/flushed skin, pink mucosa** + indoor coma → suspect CO; often absent, normal color not reassuring

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CO binds hemoglobin avidly, reduces oxygen carriage, shifts dissociation curve left
Mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation add tissue injury; fetal hemoglobin retains CO longer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous or arterial co-oximetry** measures carboxyhemoglobin; draw promptly without delaying oxygen
★ **Normal pulse oximetry and PaO₂ do not exclude poisoning**; both can appear reassuring
COHb >2% in nonsmokers or >9% in smokers supports exposure; level poorly predicts outcome
ECG, troponin for cardiac injury; lactate/ABG for acidosis; pregnancy testing when relevant
Prior oxygen or delayed presentation lowers COHb; exposure history remains decisive

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove from source, protect rescuers, assess airway and ventilation
★ **100% oxygen by nonrebreather** immediately; intubate for coma or respiratory failure
Consider hyperbaric oxygen for neurologic impairment, loss of consciousness, cardiac injury, severe acidosis, or COHb >25–30%
Pregnancy → urgent hyperbaric consultation at lower severity/levels; treatment decisions integrate symptoms, not COHb alone
Smoke inhalation + profound lactic acidosis/shock → consider cyanide, give hydroxocobalamin

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, death; delayed cognitive, behavioral, gait, or movement deficits after recovery
Follow-up for delayed neurologic symptoms; mild initial presentation does not exclude later deficits

rows.label: Prevention
items: Working CO detectors, professional heater inspection, never run generators or engines indoors
Public safety evaluation before returning to the exposure site

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral illness: fever and infectious contacts rather than shared building exposure
Methemoglobinemia: cyanosis, saturation near 85%, chocolate-colored blood
Cyanide poisoning: rapid collapse, marked lactate elevation after enclosed fire

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax** (painless curtain-like monocular vision loss), contralateral weakness, aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion
Retinal **Hollenhorst plaque** (cholesterol embolus) → ulcerated ipsilateral carotid plaque

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Hyperperfusion after revascularization → headache, seizures, brain hemorrhage; driven by **postoperative hypertension**
New deficit after endarterectomy → **noncontrast head CT** first: hemorrhage vs carotid thrombosis; no heparin/tPA beforehand
★ Expanding neck hematoma with stridor → **open wound/emergent neck exploration**; no imaging delay

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms
Giant cell arteritis: headache, jaw claudication, ↑ESR; vision loss often persistent

cervical-artery-dissection.name: Cervical artery dissection
cervical-artery-dissection.scope: Carotid artery dissection, vertebral artery dissection, Horner syndrome, posterior circulation stroke, imaging, antithrombotic therapy
cervical-artery-dissection.core: Young or middle-aged adult with sudden unilateral head or neck pain followed by retinal or cerebral ischemia after minor neck trauma.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Neck manipulation, hyperextension, sporting injury, coughing; spontaneous cases common
Fibromuscular dysplasia, connective-tissue disorders, migraine, recent infection

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Painful partial Horner syndrome**: ptosis + miosis, often without facial anhidrosis
Carotid: monocular visual loss, aphasia, contralateral weakness; pulsatile tinnitus possible
Vertebral: occipital pain, ataxia, vertigo; **lateral medullary syndrome** (crossed sensory loss, hoarseness, Horner)
Pain may precede ischemia by hours or days; normal initial neurologic examination does not exclude dissection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intimal tear or vasa vasorum hemorrhage → intramural hematoma and arterial narrowing
Mural thrombus embolization usually causes stroke; expansion may compress adjacent sympathetic fibers

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CTA head and neck** rapidly evaluates carotid/vertebral lumen and associated occlusion
MRA with fat-suppressed neck MRI identifies mural hematoma; brain MRI detects infarction
Tapered stenosis, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm support diagnosis; catheter angiography for equivocal/interventional cases
Do not rely on carotid ultrasound alone for distal carotid or vertebral lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Eligible acute ischemic stroke → **IV thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy**; dissection alone is no exclusion
★ Extracranial dissection → **antiplatelet or anticoagulation for 3–6 months**, individualized bleeding/ischemic risk
Repeat vascular imaging guides follow-up; no proven universal superiority of anticoagulation
Recurrent ischemia despite medical treatment or critical hemodynamic compromise → specialist consideration of stenting
Intracranial extension/subarachnoid hemorrhage → urgent neurovascular consultation; avoid reflex anticoagulation

rows.label: Complications
items: TIA, retinal infarction, ischemic stroke, dissecting pseudoaneurysm
Intracranial dissections may rupture into subarachnoid space; recurrent extracranial events uncommon

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid neck manipulation/contact injury while healing; control vascular risks
High-risk connective-tissue disease → individualized long-term activity counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cluster headache: episodic autonomic headache without persistent ischemic findings
Pancoast tumor: gradual Horner syndrome with shoulder/arm symptoms
BPPV: brief positional vertigo without focal deficits or acute neck pain

cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.name: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.scope: Ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, esophageal varices, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma screening
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.core: Cirrhosis produces portal hypertension and synthetic failure; new ascites, bleeding, confusion or kidney injury signals decompensation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol, chronic HBV/HCV, metabolic steatotic liver disease; autoimmune/cholestatic disorders

rows.label: Clues
items: Splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, spider angiomas, jaundice, muscle wasting
Encephalopathy: **asterixis**; triggers GI bleeding, infection, constipation, sedatives, hypokalemia, protein load
SBP may present only with subtle confusion or renal deterioration; fever/pain can be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fibrosis raises intrahepatic resistance; splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume
Portal collaterals bleed; impaired toxin clearance causes neuropsychiatric dysfunction
SBP: **intestinal bacterial translocation** into ascitic fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New/worsening or hospitalized ascites → **diagnostic paracentesis**; PMN **≥250/µL** → treat SBP
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL supports portal hypertension; send ascitic culture in bedside blood-culture bottles
HRS-AKI: exclude shock, nephrotoxins, obstruction and structural injury; assess volume response
MELD-Na/MELD 3.0 guides prognosis/transplant assessment
Encephalopathy clinical: **ammonia** not diagnostic; older exam questions may expect serum ammonia after normal head CT

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Variceal bleed → resuscitate, **octreotide + ceftriaxone**, urgent endoscopic banding; refractory → TIPS
Ascites → sodium restriction, spironolactone ± furosemide; tense ascites → paracentesis, albumin if >5 L
★ SBP → **ceftriaxone**, albumin for high-risk renal/liver dysfunction; reassess response
Encephalopathy → lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day, rifaximin (add for recurrence); correct trigger; no sedatives
HRS → stop diuretics/nephrotoxins, **terlipressin + albumin** after volume assessment; monitor hypoxia; transplant evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: HCC, recurrent infection, malnutrition, hepatopulmonary syndrome; TIPS can worsen encephalopathy
Avoid NSAIDs, sedatives and unnecessary fluid loading; INR alone poorly predicts procedural bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Ultrasound + AFP every 6 months** for HCC surveillance in eligible cirrhosis
Carvedilol for clinically significant portal hypertension when tolerated; banding if indicated and beta blocker unsuitable
After SBP → antibiotic prophylaxis; alcohol abstinence, hepatitis vaccines, adequate protein intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiac ascites: high SAAG with ascitic protein ≥2.5 g/dL
Malignant/TB ascites: usually low SAAG

delirium.name: Delirium
delirium.scope: Diagnostic criteria, precipitating causes (infection, metabolic, drugs), workup, management and prevention
delirium.core: Acute fluctuating inattention with altered cognition or awareness indicates delirium and requires a search for physiologic triggers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, baseline dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, hospitalization or recent surgery
Infection (UTI, pneumonia, wound), hypoxia, metabolic derangement, dehydration, retention, constipation and uncontrolled pain
Anticholinergics (amitriptyline), meperidine, other opioids, steroids, sedatives; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal

rows.label: Clues
items: Disorganized thinking, sleep–wake reversal, hallucinations; hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed presentation
★ Hypoactive withdrawal/lethargy easily missed; **test attention**, not orientation alone
Digit span, months backward or inability to sustain conversation reveals attentional deficit
**Asterixis** → toxic-metabolic encephalopathy of any cause, not only hepatic failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Systemic stress and drug effects disrupt vulnerable brain networks and neurotransmitter balance
Multiple small precipitating factors can exceed low cognitive reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CAM**: acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Immediate glucose, oxygenation, vitals; focused neurologic examination, medication review and collateral baseline
CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function; ECG, chest imaging guided by findings; wound/sepsis signs → **blood cultures**
CT head for focal deficit, trauma or unexplained reduced consciousness; LP for suspected CNS infection
Fever, urinary symptoms or dementia → **urinalysis** for UTI before CT/LP; bacteriuria alone doesn't prove cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat precipitant**; reorient, restore hearing/glasses, hydrate, mobilize and normalize sleep
Calm environment and familiar support; remove unnecessary catheters and avoid physical restraints
★ Severe distress or danger despite de-escalation → short course **haloperidol**, check QT/EPS risk
Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia → avoid potent dopamine blockers; specialist-guided alternative
Benzodiazepines generally worsen delirium; reserve for withdrawal or selected seizures/catatonia

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, persistent cognitive impairment and increased mortality
Antipsychotics may prolong QT; sedation may conceal clinical deterioration

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Multicomponent prevention: orientation, daytime activity, sleep protection, hydration, pain control and drug review
Minimize nighttime interruptions and unnecessary sedatives; encourage family engagement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: chronic progression; attention relatively preserved early
Depression: sustained mood symptoms without fluctuating consciousness
Primary psychosis: usually preserved attention and alertness

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; somatic presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication
Youth: **irritable mood** qualifies; academic decline, withdrawal, somatic complaints; not normal teenage behavior

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, **HPA hyperactivity with raised cortisol**, and neuroplasticity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
Screen all adults, even asymptomatic: PHQ-2, PHQ-9 for severity; older adults: **Geriatric Depression Scale**
Interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk
Post-CABG anhedonia, withdrawal, fatigue → depression screen; vein-harvest leg edema expected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger or **severe malnutrition** → **observation, psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal therapy; moderate/severe: sertraline + psychotherapy; pregnancy → shared risk–benefit discussion
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Alternatives: **bupropion** (fatigue/hypersomnia, smoking cessation), **mirtazapine** (poor appetite, insomnia)
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid with eating disorders, seizure disorders or brain tumor; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation
Benzodiazepines in older adults: worsen depression, sedation, falls → stop, use antidepressant

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after drug changes
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; **pseudodementia**: subacute, "I don't know" answers, recall improves with prompting
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH
Untreated OSA: snoring, obesity, sleepiness → **mood disorder due to medical condition**, not MDD
Anorexia nervosa: fear of weight gain, distorted body image

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

dystonia.name: Dystonia
dystonia.scope: Focal dystonia (cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, writer's cramp), generalized dystonia, dopa-responsive dystonia, sensory tricks (geste antagoniste), botulinum toxin injections, trihexyphenidyl
dystonia.core: Sustained or intermittent patterned muscle contractions create twisting movements and abnormal postures, sometimes specific to a task.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Inherited early-onset syndromes; dopamine-blocking antipsychotics or antiemetics; structural basal ganglia disease
Adult-onset disease often focal; childhood onset more likely to generalize

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Sensory trick**: light touch transiently improves abnormal posture; supports dystonia
Cervical dystonia: torticollis, neck pain; blepharospasm: bilateral involuntary eyelid closure
Writer's cramp: task-specific hand posturing; overflow activation during voluntary movement
★ Childhood leg dystonia **worse later in day**, better after sleep → dopa-responsive disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired motor inhibition within basal ganglia/cerebellar networks → co-contraction of opposing muscles

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical phenomenology** plus drug history and full neurologic examination
Early-onset unexplained dystonia → levodopa trial; consider genetic testing
MRI for rapid onset, focal neurologic abnormalities or suspected secondary lesion
Young person with dystonia and psychiatric/hepatic findings → ceruloplasmin, urine copper, slit-lamp examination

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Focal disabling dystonia → **botulinum toxin** into affected muscles
Generalized symptoms → trihexyphenidyl, baclofen or clonazepam; monitor cognitive/anticholinergic adverse effects
Dopa-responsive disease → sustained benefit from low-dose levodopa/carbidopa
Acute drug-induced dystonia → stop culprit, IV/IM diphenhydramine or benztropine; airway first if laryngeal involvement
Severe refractory generalized disease → globus pallidus DBS; rehabilitation supports function

rows.label: Complications
items: Pain, contractures, impaired vision/writing/swallowing; botulinum toxin may cause local weakness or dysphagia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid re-exposure to culprit dopamine blockers; use lowest necessary exposure in susceptible individuals
Stretching and occupational adaptations reduce secondary disability

rows.label: Mimics
items: Tics: premonitory urge, partial suppressibility, brief nonfixed movements
Spasticity: velocity-dependent tone with UMN signs
Functional dystonia: positive inconsistency/incongruence; diagnosis not based solely on normal imaging

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.scope: Focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, EEG findings, antiepileptic therapy (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine), lifestyle counseling
epilepsy.core: Recurrent unprovoked seizures reflect epilepsy; classify focal versus generalized onset before choosing a maintenance antiseizure drug.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, developmental lesions, genetic predisposition
Sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal and missed drugs can precipitate seizures; provoked seizures alone ≠ epilepsy

rows.label: Clues
items: Focal onset: aura, unilateral motor activity, automatisms or impaired awareness; may evolve bilaterally
Generalized tonic-clonic: abrupt loss of consciousness, stiffening/jerking, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury
Absence: staring, immediate recovery; JME: morning myoclonus ± generalized convulsions
Infantile spasms: flexion clusters, **hypsarrhythmia** on EEG; standard antiseizure drugs ineffective

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormally synchronized cortical neuronal discharges impair awareness, sensation or motor function
Excitatory/inhibitory imbalance may arise from structural lesions or inherited channel/network dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI** after unprovoked seizure; normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy
Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, or one with high recurrence risk/defined syndrome
Check glucose/electrolytes and provoking causes; urgent CT for trauma, focal deficit or persistent altered consciousness
Absence: generalized **3-Hz spike-wave**, provoked by hyperventilation; JME: generalized polyspike-wave
Child, nocturnal facial twitching/drooling, speech arrest + **centrotemporal spikes** → benign rolandic epilepsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Convulsion **≥5 minutes** → airway/glucose, **lorazepam**, then IV levetiracetam/fosphenytoin/valproate
Focal epilepsy → lamotrigine or levetiracetam; generalized tonic-clonic/JME → broad-spectrum agent
★ Valproate effective for generalized syndromes; **avoid when pregnancy possible** if alternatives effective
Pure absence → ethosuximide; absence + tonic-clonic → broad-spectrum drug; infantile spasms → **ACTH or vigabatrin**
Avoid carbamazepine/phenytoin for absence/myoclonic syndromes; drug-resistant focal disease → surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Status epilepticus, injury, aspiration, SUDEP; valproate → hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity
Lamotrigine → serious rash with rapid titration
Levetiracetam → irritability/mood symptoms; depression history + high recurrence risk → continue, monitor mood
Erythromycin (CYP3A4 inhibitor) ↑carbamazepine → ataxia, somnolence, diplopia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adherence, regular sleep, avoid alcohol excess; no abrupt drug withdrawal
Driving restrictions follow local law; no unsupervised swimming/heights; preconception folate and drug review
Pregnancy lowers antiseizure levels; breakthrough seizures → **increase current drug dose**, avoid switching

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syncope: prodrome, rapid recovery; brief jerks possible
Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG confirms typical event without epileptic correlate

table.title: Focal seizure localization
rows: Epigastric/olfactory aura, lip-smacking automatisms; superior quadrantanopia

epilepsy.evidence: Pregnancy recommendations checked 2026-10-30: [AAN/AES/SMFM 2024](https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/5170); classification established teaching.

essential-tremor.name: Essential tremor
essential-tremor.scope: Postural and kinetic bilateral action tremor, hands and head tremor, alcohol responsiveness, absence of parkinsonian features, propranolol, primidone, topiramate, deep brain stimulation
essential-tremor.core: Gradual bilateral hand shaking during posture or action, often with a familial pattern and temporary improvement after alcohol.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history often autosomal dominant; prevalence rises with age

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Action tremor**, impaired writing/pouring; head or voice may also be affected
No bradykinesia, rigidity, focal weakness, sensory loss or cerebellar gait dysfunction
Usually symmetric; finger-to-nose tremor without true dysmetria

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal oscillation within cerebellothalamocortical networks; no single routine diagnostic biomarker

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical examination**: observe rest, outstretched arms, handwriting/spiral drawing and goal-directed movement
Review beta-agonists, stimulants, lithium, valproate; TSH if hyperthyroidism possible
MRI reserved for abrupt onset, focal deficits, marked asymmetry or other atypical features

rows.label: Tx
items: Mild symptoms → reassurance, adaptive utensils, reduce triggers
★ Function-limiting hand tremor → **propranolol or primidone**; combination if partial response
Propranolol: avoid with asthma, symptomatic bradycardia or heart block; primidone: sedation/ataxia
Persistent symptoms → topiramate; selected head/voice tremor → botulinum toxin
★ Severe drug-refractory disability → **thalamic DBS** or selected focused ultrasound thalamotomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Difficulty eating, writing, grooming; social embarrassment and occupational limitations
Treatment-related fatigue, hypotension, cognitive slowing; botulinum toxin can cause focal weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established disease prevention; minimize caffeine and sleep deprivation to reduce exacerbations
Avoid alcohol as chronic treatment because of dependence and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Parkinson disease: asymmetric resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity
Enhanced physiologic tremor: fine, trigger-related; resolves with cause correction
Cerebellar tremor: intention worsening with dysmetria, nystagmus or ataxia

essential-tremor.evidence: Not checked online; established movement-disorder diagnosis and treatment teaching.

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection 2–4 weeks post-exposure: fever, rash, sore throat, **mucosal ulcers**, diarrhea, generalized lymphadenopathy
Weight loss, thrush, recurrent candida/herpes, **extensive adult molluscum** → test HIV; dysphagia → candidal esophagitis
Child/teen: chronic fever/diarrhea, poor growth, generalized nodes, splenomegaly, **polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB, pregnancy testing, **cervical cytology**
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count
Prenatal: opt-out screening; refusal → counsel, re-offer later; never test without consent

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: **pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin**, else TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, ophthalmology
Untreated/viremic mother's newborn → **triple ART** ASAP, ideally within 6 h, ≤6 weeks; suppressed mother → zidovudine alone

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary lesion; biopsy after failed empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment, earlier if serology/imaging/CSF PCR disagree
SCID/CVID: low immunoglobulins; SCID lymphopenia, no nodes; perinatal HIV: PJP, thrush, nodes, normal lymphocytes

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; sputum/BAL silver stain
Ring-enhancing mass lesions, edema/mass effect; positive IgG
Cognitive decline; non-enhancing subcortical demyelination, no mass effect

huntington-disease.name: Huntington disease
huntington-disease.scope: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, anticipation, chorea, caudate and putamen atrophy, psychiatric manifestations
huntington-disease.core: An inherited progressive movement, cognitive, and psychiatric disorder often emerges in midlife, with earlier onset across successive generations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Autosomal dominant HTT CAG expansion**; each child of an affected heterozygote has 50% risk
Paternal transmission particularly associated with repeat expansion and anticipation

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular flowing chorea, motor impersistence, impaired voluntary saccades; later rigidity and bradykinesia
Irritability, depression, impulsivity, psychosis; executive dysfunction progresses to dementia
Psychiatric symptoms may precede movement disorder; juvenile disease often rigid with seizures
★ **Suicidal ideation** requires direct safety assessment, especially around diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Toxic huntingtin damages striatal GABAergic neurons; reduced indirect-pathway inhibition increases unwanted movement
Caudate/putamen atrophy produces enlarged frontal horns on brain imaging

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Compatible phenotype/family history → **HTT genetic testing** after informed counseling
≥40 repeats: full penetrance; 36–39: reduced penetrance; intermediate alleles can expand in offspring
MRI supports differential diagnosis; gene testing confirms, imaging alone does not
Predictive testing of asymptomatic adults → consent, psychological assessment and genetic counseling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling chorea → **tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine**; monitor depression, suicidality and parkinsonism
Antipsychotics such as risperidone for psychosis/aggression; SSRIs for depression/anxiety
Physical/occupational and speech-swallow support; nutrition, fall prevention and advance-care planning
No established cure; avoid dopamine-depleting agents in active suicidality or inadequately treated depression

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, falls, weight loss, loss of independence; suicide
VMAT2 inhibitors → sedation, akathisia, depression; antipsychotics → metabolic and motor adverse effects

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reproductive counseling, prenatal/preimplantation testing options; defer predictive testing of asymptomatic minors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Wilson disease: younger onset, liver disease, low ceruloplasmin; potentially treatable
Tardive dyskinesia: dopamine-blocker exposure, predominant orobuccolingual stereotypies

huntington-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage (most common) or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids/vitamin A supplements

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late, compensatory; treat ICP, not BP
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema
IIH: **impaired CSF resorption** at arachnoid granulations; ventricles normal/small, no obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings → **LP**: normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction
Recent shunt revision + fever + neutrophilic CSF → **shunt infection**, not community meningitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway/intubation first**, head elevation, IV **hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation and reflexes generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
Proximal weakness + ↑CK → EMG/nerve conduction (myopathic pattern); MRI guides **muscle biopsy**
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs
Guillain-Barré: ascending distal-predominant weakness, areflexia

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

insomnia.name: Insomnia
insomnia.scope: Chronic insomnia, sleep hygiene, stimulus control therapy, sleep restriction, delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, pharmacotherapy indications
insomnia.core: Persistent difficulty sleeping despite adequate opportunity, with daytime impairment, calls for CBT-I and evaluation of perpetuating causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Stress, depression/anxiety, chronic pain, irregular schedules, conditioned worry about sleep
Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stimulants, glucocorticoids; older age and menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep or early awakening, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability
★ Chronic disorder: **≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months**, with adequate sleep opportunity
Delayed phase: late sleep/wake times but normal sleep quality and duration when schedule unrestricted
Loud snoring, witnessed apnea, irresistible sleepiness, or restless legs suggests another sleep disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cognitive/physiologic hyperarousal and learned bed–wake association perpetuate insomnia
Circadian phase delay misaligns internal timing with required social schedule

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Sleep history and 1–2-week diary**; review schedule, substances, mood, pain, and medications
Polysomnography: suspected apnea, limb movements, unusual behaviors, or refractory uncertainty; not routine
Actigraphy can clarify circadian timing; assess bipolar disorder before sleep-restriction interventions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CBT-I first-line**: stimulus control, sleep restriction/compression, cognitive restructuring, relaxation
Stimulus control: bed only for sleep/sex; leave when persistently awake, return when sleepy
Restrict time in bed to consolidate sleep, then expand; fixed wake time and avoid naps
★ **Sleep hygiene alone insufficient**; reduce evening stimulants, alcohol, screens; dark quiet room
Short-term: doxepin, ramelteon, orexin antagonist; acute stressor → **zolpidem**; maintenance + dysphoria → **trazodone**

rows.label: Complications
items: Impaired driving/work, low mood; hypnotics, especially benzodiazepines (alprazolam) → falls, cognitive impairment, dependence
Z-drugs can cause complex sleep behaviors; avoid sedative combinations and routine antihistamines in older adults

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain regular wake time and daytime activity; address pain/mood disorders and relapse triggers
★ Delayed phase → **fixed daily bed and wake times**, morning bright light, evening melatonin, gradual advance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Insufficient sleep: inadequate opportunity, improves with longer sleep duration
Mania: reduced need for sleep with increased energy, rather than distressing fatigue
OSA: sleep fragmentation with snoring/apneas; coexistence possible

intracranial-hemorrhage.name: Intracranial hemorrhage
intracranial-hemorrhage.scope: Intracerebral hemorrhage, hypertensive hemorrhage, amyloid angiopathy, coagulopathy reversal, blood pressure management
intracranial-hemorrhage.core: Acute focal neurologic deficits with headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness require immediate CT to identify intraparenchymal bleeding and guide reversal.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Chronic hypertension, older age, anticoagulants/coagulopathy, stimulant use
Vascular malformation, tumor, venous thrombosis; lobar recurrence in older adults suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid progression, seizure, severe BP elevation; small bleeds may resemble ischemic stroke
★ Hypertensive sites: **putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum**; amyloid favors superficial lobar locations
Declining consciousness, asymmetric pupils, abnormal posturing → mass effect/herniation
Cerebellar injury: vomiting, severe ataxia, vertigo; rapid deterioration possible despite initially preserved alertness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Small-artery lipohyalinosis or amyloid deposition weakens vessel walls
Expanding hematoma, intraventricular extension, and perihematomal edema cause secondary injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast head CT now**; CBC/platelets, INR/PTT, renal function, glucose, medication history
CTA/vascular imaging for younger patients, atypical location, suspected malformation; repeat CT for deterioration/expansion
MRI susceptibility imaging identifies microbleeds and underlying lesions after stabilization
Do not give thrombolysis or perform LP for established parenchymal hemorrhage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway, head elevation, neuro-ICU; **stop anticoagulants and reverse immediately**
★ Mild/moderate ICH, SBP 150–220 → IV **nicardipine/clevidipine**, target ~140, maintain 130–150 mm Hg
Large/severe ICH requires individualized perfusion goals; avoid abrupt excessive BP reduction or SBP <130
Cerebellar deterioration, hydrocephalus, brainstem compression, or volume ≥15 mL → **urgent surgical evacuation**
Hydrocephalus → ventricular drain; herniation → hypertonic saline/mannitol; treat seizures, no routine prophylaxis

rows.label: Complications
items: Hematoma expansion, hydrocephalus, herniation, seizures, disability, recurrent hemorrhage
★ **No routine platelet transfusion** for antiplatelet-associated ICH without emergency surgery/severe thrombocytopenia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Long-term BP control, smoking/stimulant cessation; reassess anticoagulation using recurrence and embolic risks
Intermittent pneumatic compression immediately; low-dose heparin prophylaxis after bleeding stability is documented

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ischemic stroke: no acute blood on CT; SAH: thunderclap, sulcal/cisternal blood
Hemorrhagic tumor: mass/edema pattern, enhancement; confirm with MRI

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness means retinal embolism from the ipsilateral carotid.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Hypertension: greatest modifiable risk factor**; smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: **Broca** nonfluent, poor repetition, intact comprehension; **Wernicke** fluent paraphasias, poor comprehension, no insight
Crossed: **Weber** ipsilateral CN III, contralateral hemiparesis (midbrain); lateral pons: ipsilateral full-face palsy, deafness
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction, often embolic; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF/cardioembolic → oral anticoagulation, timing by infarct/bleeding risk; noncardioembolic → antiplatelet only
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit
Long-term antiplatelet (aspirin allergy → clopidogrel); undertreated hypertension → **intensify antihypertensives**; high-intensity statin

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

table.title: Vascular localization
rows: Occipital: contralateral homonymous hemianopia; macular sparing
Diplopia, vertigo, dysarthria, ataxia, crossed/bilateral signs, coma
Vertigo; ipsilateral Horner/face/ataxia/palate; contralateral body pain-temperature

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, no heavy lifting until pain resolves, heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical therapy if pain persists despite NSAIDs; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise
Vascular claudication: calf pain, bicycling too; standing still relieves; weak pulses alone don't exclude stenosis

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates
Shopping-cart sign; pulses usually preserved; MRI confirms

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

macrocytic-anemia.name: Macrocytic anemia
macrocytic-anemia.scope: Folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
macrocytic-anemia.core: MCV >100 fL prompts separation of megaloblastic DNA-synthesis failure from alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, and marrow disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Vegan diet without supplementation, gastric bypass, ileal disease/resection, metformin, long-term **PPI** → B12 depletion
Alcohol misuse, poor intake, pregnancy, methotrexate, trimethoprim → folate depletion; stores last months, B12 years
Autoimmune gastritis → pernicious anemia; nitrous oxide functionally inactivates cobalamin

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, glossitis; ineffective erythropoiesis may raise LDH/indirect bilirubin and lower other cell lines
★ **Paresthesias, gait ataxia, impaired vibration/proprioception** → B12 deficiency, even without anemia
Smooth macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils indicate megaloblastic change

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective thymidine synthesis delays nuclear maturation relative to cytoplasm
B12-dependent myelin metabolism explains spinal cord/peripheral nerve injury; folate deficiency lacks this syndrome
B12 malabsorption corrected by oral intrinsic factor → **gastric IF loss** (atrophic gastritis), not ileal disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, smear, reticulocytes, B12**; assess folate, liver tests, TSH, exposures
Borderline B12 → methylmalonic acid; renal impairment can elevate it independently
★ Suspected pernicious anemia → **anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies**; highly specific but not fully sensitive
High reticulocytes → bleeding/hemolysis; unexplained cytopenias/dysplasia → bone marrow evaluation for MDS
Coexisting iron deficiency may normalize MCV; neurologic suspicion still requires B12 evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Replace B12 before or with folate**; folate alone can conceal ongoing neurologic injury
Neurologic/severe deficiency or malabsorption → parenteral B12 initially; irreversible cause requires lifelong replacement
Dietary B12 deficiency may respond to high-dose oral replacement; folate deficiency → oral folic acid
Remove causative drug/exposure where possible; monitor reticulocyte response and count recovery

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated B12 deficiency → irreversible neurologic disability; severe disease → pancytopenia
Pernicious anemia → increased gastric adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumor risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reliable B12 supplementation for vegans**; lifelong monitoring/replacement after relevant GI surgery
Folic acid before conception and early pregnancy; improve nutrition and reduce harmful alcohol intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol-associated macrocytosis: round macrocytes, no required megaloblastic change
Myelodysplasia: persistent multilineage cytopenia, dysplastic marrow
Reticulocytosis: polychromasia after blood loss or hemolysis

macrocytic-anemia.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology and nutritional teaching.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adults: **S. pneumoniae** most common; seeded by pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis, CSF leak, asplenia
Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; advanced HIV/transplant/chemotherapy → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: subacute, high opening pressure ± CN VI palsy, CSF antigen; TB studies if lymphocytic, low glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal contacts within 7 days of onset → **rifampin or ceftriaxone**; droplet isolation until 24 hours treated
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

mononeuropathies.name: Mononeuropathies
mononeuropathies.scope: Ulnar nerve entrapment (cubital tunnel, Guyon canal, claw hand), radial nerve palsy (wrist drop, Saturday night palsy), peroneal/fibular nerve injury (foot drop), electromyography, splinting, surgical decompression
mononeuropathies.core: Weakness and sensory loss following one peripheral nerve suggest focal compression or injury; preserved muscles supplied proximally help localize the lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Compression, fractures, repetitive motion, tight casts, diabetes; intoxicated immobilization → Saturday night radial palsy
Prolonged elbow flexion, cycling/hypothenar pressure, leg crossing, rapid weight loss
Lithotomy/hip hyperflexion → **femoral** under inguinal ligament; stirrup at fibular head → foot drop
Antecubital hematoma after venipuncture → **median at elbow**; hook of hamate fracture → ulnar in Guyon canal

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Ulnar: **Froment sign**, advanced fourth/fifth-digit clawing; impaired grip and fine finger tasks
Rapid progression, severe pain, multiple noncontiguous nerves → consider vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex
Supraspinatus/infraspinatus atrophy, sensation intact, overhead athlete → **suprascapular** entrapment
Medial plantar laceration → medial toe hyperextension; superficial radial → dorsal web numbness, no wrist drop

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal compression first causes conduction block/demyelination; severe or sustained pressure causes axonal loss
Axonal regeneration is slow; duration and severity predict recovery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Map strength, reflexes, and sensation; compare muscles sharing a root but supplied by different nerves
Persistent/uncertain deficit → **EMG/nerve conduction studies**; denervation may take weeks to appear
Trauma → radiographs; suspected mass/structural entrapment → ultrasound or MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove compression; activity modification, **splinting**, occupational/physical rehabilitation
Ulnar at elbow → night extension splint; radial palsy → wrist-extension splint
Foot drop → ankle-foot orthosis and gait training; inspect cast/brace pressure points
★ Progressive deficit/refractory entrapment → **surgical decompression**; nerve laceration → urgent repair evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Muscle atrophy, fixed contractures, chronic neuropathic pain, falls
Delayed recognition of ongoing compression → irreversible motor deficit

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged elbow pressure, excessive flexion, leg crossing; pad vulnerable areas during surgery/immobility
Optimize diabetes control; ergonomic adjustment and frequent position changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: L5 radiculopathy: root-pattern pain; weakness also in tibialis posterior and gluteus medius
C8 radiculopathy: additional median-innervated muscle weakness, proximal symptoms
Stroke: sudden deficit with upper motor neuron signs or additional central findings

table.title: Localize common lesions
rows: Ulnar hand intrinsics; forearm spared; wrist Tinel
Palmar ulnar digits; dorsal hand spared
Finger extension; wrist extension partly preserved

mononeuropathies.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.name: Neuromuscular junction disorders
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.scope: Myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism, repetitive nerve stimulation, autoantibodies
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.core: Fluctuating or descending weakness with preserved sensation localizes to neuromuscular transmission; reflexes, pupils, and exercise response separate major causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: MG: autoimmune disease, thymoma; LEMS: smoking/small-cell lung carcinoma
Botulism: improperly canned foods, injection wounds, infant honey or environmental spores

rows.label: Clues
items: MG: diplopia, ptosis, nasal speech, chewing fatigue; worse late day or repeated activity
LEMS: proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation; transient strength/reflex improvement after exertion
Botulism: cranial palsies → symmetric descending paralysis, autonomic dysfunction; infant constipation and floppy weakness
★ **Bulbar weakness or declining ventilation** → impending respiratory failure even with normal oxygen saturation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: MG: postsynaptic receptor/MuSK autoimmunity; LEMS: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel autoimmunity
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → impaired acetylcholine release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AChR antibodies**, then MuSK if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG
MG → chest CT for thymoma; bedside ice-pack improvement supports ocular disease
LEMS → P/Q calcium-channel antibodies and chest CT for cancer
★ Suspected crisis → serial **forced vital capacity/negative inspiratory force**; not pulse oximetry alone
Botulism → serum/stool/toxin testing via public health; treatment before confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: MG → pyridostigmine, steroid-sparing immunosuppression; thymectomy for thymoma or selected generalized AChR-positive disease
★ Myasthenic crisis → **airway support + IVIG or plasma exchange**, treat precipitant
LEMS → amifampridine and treatment of malignancy; immunotherapy for persistent autoimmune disease
★ Botulism → **heptavalent antitoxin**; infants → human botulism immune globulin; ventilatory support
Wound botulism → debridement/antibiotics; avoid aminoglycosides and magnesium with impaired junctional transmission

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, respiratory arrest; MG immunosuppression → infection; steroids may initially worsen weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review MG-exacerbating drugs; safe food preservation; no honey before age 1 year
LEMS → ongoing cancer surveillance if initial evaluation negative

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: usually ascending weakness and areflexia, possible sensory symptoms
Brainstem stroke: abrupt focal signs; motor neuron disease: fasciculations/UMN signs

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.evidence: Botulism checked 2026-10-30: [CDC clinical guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7002a1.htm); MG/LEMS: established teaching.

parkinson-disease.name: Parkinson disease
parkinson-disease.scope: Cardinal motor symptoms (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability/pull test), nonmotor symptoms, dopamine agonists, levodopa-carbidopa, atypical parkinsonism (PSP, MSA)
parkinson-disease.core: Progressive asymmetric bradykinesia with characteristic motor signs and levodopa responsiveness suggests Parkinson disease; early atypical features prompt another diagnosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, family susceptibility, some pesticide exposures; most disease sporadic
Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics/metoclopramide cause secondary parkinsonism rather than idiopathic disease
MPTP (synthetic heroin contaminant) → rapid parkinsonism from nigral dopaminergic neuron destruction

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity**, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait
Freezing, micrographia, hypophonia; pull test reveals impaired postural recovery, typically later
Constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression and autonomic symptoms can precede motor disease
Early severe falls, gaze palsy, marked autonomic failure or poor treatment response → atypical syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss; α-synuclein Lewy bodies
Reduced striatal dopamine disrupts basal ganglia motor regulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity
Brain MRI for atypical findings; dopamine transporter imaging if uncertain degenerative versus nondegenerative tremor
Review medications; assess cognition, orthostatic BP, gait and swallowing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Function-limiting motor symptoms → **carbidopa/levodopa**, preferred initial dopaminergic treatment
Pramipexole/ropinirole for selected younger patients; avoid with hallucinations, impulse-control problems or age >70
Wearing-off → adjust levodopa schedule, add MAO-B/COMT inhibitor; dyskinesia → amantadine
★ Exercise, PT/speech/swallow rehab; refractory fluctuations/tremor/dyskinesias → **deep brain stimulation**, pallidotomy
Psychosis → reduce provoking drugs; pimavanserin or selected quetiapine/clozapine, avoid potent dopamine blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, dementia; medication → hallucinations, orthostasis, motor fluctuations/dyskinesias
Dopamine agonists → gambling/hypersexuality and sleep attacks; abrupt withdrawal → severe rigidity/hyperthermia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall-proof home, medication adherence, aspiration-risk assessment; no established primary neuroprotective treatment

rows.label: Mimics
